children: As Americans vote to decide who will control Congress, Asia markets are bracing for an outcome that could have major implications for policymaking in the world's largest economy.

Top of mind is how the midterm results will shape U.S. policy around tariffs, fiscal measures that have a bearing on artificial-intelligence spending and the prospect of a diplomatic resolution in the Middle East.
As polls close, here's what to watch:

BLUE SWEEP: Many predictions markets see Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate as the most likely outcome--one that could complicate the administration's capacity to push through policy.

A decisive Democrat win could be negative for equities, U.S. Treasury yields and the dollar by virtue of pushback against AI and data centers, a slightly weaker U.S. growth outlook and perhaps the possibility that confrontations between President Trump against Democrats increase, said Eric C. Robertsen, global head of research & chief strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

LIGHT BLUE: Some observers think prediction sites are overestimating the degree of a Democratic win, expecting a "gridlock" scenario instead where Republicans hold the Senate and Democrats take the House.

MUFG's U.S. Macro Strategy team sees that as the most market-friendly outcome, as a divided government would limit policy changes while preserving AI investment. In that event, they expect a decent equity rally and a muted bond reaction as traders refocus on underlying trends. Under an unlikely Republican sweep, "stocks would rip and bonds would dip."

AI ANGST: AI spending has been the lifeblood of many Asian markets and economies this year, offsetting the hit from the U.S.-Iran war oil shock. A shift in power in Washington perceived as negative for AI momentum could hurt sentiment.

Asia's AI infrastructure players--from Taiwanese and South Korean chip titans to Japan's semiconductor-equipment makers--are heavily exposed to U.S.-led AI investment.  The distinction lies between a correction in tech valuations and an actual reduction in customer spending plans, said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy & research APAC at State Street Investment Management. "The latter would have a more direct impact on Asian earnings."
FX: Asian currencies could gain from a result that tempers the greenback on expectations of limited scope for fiscal expansion, but analysts say fundamentals will stay in the driver's seat.
The dollar continues to respond predominantly to the Federal Reserve rate expectations, which shouldn't face an immediate impact from the midterms, said ING's Francesco Pesole.

Asia FX responses will differ according to energy-import dependence, external balances and exposure to tech demand, said Liu at State Street. He cautions on treating the yen as an automatic hedge, as its response depends on risk sentiment and rate differentials, while the yuan needs to be assessed alongside China's outlook and exchange-rate management, not just the U.S. vote.
FOREIGN POLICY: As a heavily-export reliant region that imports a lot of its oil and gas, a critical focus for Asia is what the vote means for U.S. policy tariff and the Middle East.

It could be argued that a more hostile legislative backdrop may temper some external policies relating to Iran and tariffs, BNP Paribas economists said. "But there is another narrative that, unburdened by the electoral cycle, Trump may become more assertive internationally."
They suggest assuming that tensions and volatility will resume post-midterms and caution investors in Asian equities against banking on major tariff rollbacks.

Democrats gaining more control could mean more scrutiny of war policy, helping pave the way for oil prices to fall sustainably, but a weaker Republican position doesn't automatically mean a lower geopolitical risk premium, said Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya.
Ultimately, Asia is still vulnerable to higher oil and commodity prices, and that won't go away because of the midterms, StanChart's Robertsen said.
Sherry Qin and Amanda Lee contributed to this report
